# Week 31, 2026

Highlights selected from everything kept between July 24, 2026 and July 31, 2026. Items are selected nightly by an automated pipeline and the summaries are machine generated; follow the links to the original sources. See [About](../../about.md) for how selection works.

<img class="section-banner" src="../../../assets/section-digest.svg" alt="">

## The week in brief

<div class="section-brief">
<p>A multicenter randomized controlled trial in Nature Medicine reported that Retina4IRD, an artificial intelligence (AI) clinician decision support system for inherited retinal diseases, raised specialists&#x27; top-5 genetic diagnostic accuracy from 67.3% to 88.5% and improved downstream management scores compared with specialists working alone <a href="https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-026-04545-w">[1]</a>. A separate system, MACE-MAIS, predicted major adverse cardiovascular events from incomplete cardiovascular magnetic resonance and electronic health record data while attaching an interpretable rationale to each prediction <a href="https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-03008-3">[2]</a>. Both illustrate the kind of task-based clinical evidence that a Nature Medicine comment argues the field still lacks at scale; its authors contend that current benchmarks for claims of medical AI &quot;superintelligence&quot; are misleading and insufficient <a href="https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-026-04539-8">[3]</a>.</p>
<p>The stakes for teaching are drawn out in an npj Digital Medicine perspective on health professions education, which argues that generative AI intensifies rather than replaces the need for coaching, critical appraisal, self-regulation, and trustworthy assessment <a href="https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-03042-1">[4]</a>. Two items show why that appraisal skill matters in practice: a simulation study found ambient AI scribes propagated interpreter errors into clinical notes during multilingual encounters <a href="https://medinform.jmir.org/2026/1/e88734">[5]</a>, and a French cancer center&#x27;s framework for the European Union (EU) AI Act concludes that safe integration depends on institutional readiness, not algorithmic performance <a href="https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-03073-8">[6]</a>. On the tooling side, OpenAI released batch and live transcription models with custom vocabulary support relevant to clinical documentation <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WeP9VUf1OoE">[12]</a> and opened free frontier model access to 100,000 academic researchers <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MLehRytu9Zo">[9]</a>.</p>
<p class="section-brief-date">Written from the items highlighted below; numbered links go to the sources.</p>
</div>
